questions.prompt: How does the core investigative question differ in an insider threat case?
options: It is identical to every other playbook
The question is whether access exceeded authorization, not whether access occurred -- the subject legitimately had credentials
The question is only which malware was used
There is no investigative question, only an HR process
questions.explanation: Because the subject had legitimate access, 'how did they get in' is not meaningful. What matters is whether their activity exceeded what their role authorized.

questions.prompt: Why must a baseline be established before reviewing the subject's activity?
options: To satisfy a technical logging requirement
Because confirmation bias makes ambiguous activity look incriminating when you are already looking for incrimination
Because baselines are required by ATT&CK
Because activity logs are only readable in chronological order
questions.explanation: An investigation launched on suspicion will surface ambiguous activity. Establishing normal first -- for the subject and their peers -- is what makes the comparison defensible.

questions.prompt: Why is access revocation timing coordinated with HR and Legal rather than decided by IR?
options: IR has no technical ability to revoke access
Revoking access early can destroy the opportunity to establish scope, and interview and termination timing has legal implications
Legal owns all Active Directory permissions
Revocation is not part of insider investigations
questions.explanation: Premature revocation both alerts the subject and cuts off the activity you are trying to characterize, so timing is a joint decision rather than a technical one.

questions.prompt: Why does the playbook stress documenting what was NOT found?
options: Because in an investigation that may end in termination or litigation, absence of evidence is itself a finding requiring deliberate record
Because negative findings are required by ATT&CK
Because HR cannot read technical findings
questions.explanation: Where an investigation may support employment or legal action, clearly recording what was checked and found clean is as important as recording positive findings.
